book: The Way of the Bodhisattva — Selections

1: Awakening of the heart is like the flash of lightning on a night of clouds and darkness: it illumines for an instant, and then all is dark again — yet that instant outshines the longest ages of ordinary goodness. For the awakened heart is the first resolve to carry every being, without exception, across the river of suffering.

Just as the previous buddhas gave birth to the awakening of the heart and trained step by step upon the path, so shall I, for the sake of all beings, give birth to the awakening of the heart, and train step by step upon the path.

Today my birth has borne fruit; I have drawn well the meaning of this human life. Today I am born into the family of the buddhas; I am now the child of the buddhas. In whatever ways I can, I shall act so that this family is not shamed.
2: [Bodhicaryavatara III 17-18 — May I be a bridge]

May I be a guard for those who have no guard, a guide for those who journey, a boat, a raft, a bridge for those who wish to cross the flood. May I be a lamp for those who need light, a resting place for the weary, and for all beings who need a servant, may I be a slave.
[Bodhicaryavatara III 19-20 — The medicine and the tree]

May I be the doctor and the medicine, and may I be the nurse for all sick beings in the world, until the sickness of suffering is forever gone. Like the great earth and the other elements, may I be the sustenance and the foundation of innumerable beings, pervading space, for as long as they last.

To cover the earth with leather so that my feet never touch a thorn — there is not enough leather in the world. But leather on the soles of my shoes covers the whole earth. So it is with the sharpness of the world: I cannot silence every voice, but I can still my own mind, and that stilling covers everything.
3: [Bodhicaryavatara VI 96 — The patience of the wronged]

If the suffering I must bear will pass, why should I be troubled? If it will not pass, what use is anger? The enemy who harms me is himself driven by affliction; he is not master of himself. Shall I be angry with a hand that is struck, or with the affliction that wields it?

First cherish the notion of the difference between 'I' and 'other'; then dwell in the certainty that I and other are the same. I shall protect others just as I protect myself, for their suffering is real to them, as mine is real to me — and there is no difference in the feeling of pain.

By the virtue I have gathered, may all beings be freed from pain. May the blind see forms, the deaf hear sounds, and may the naked find clothing, the hungry food, and the thirsty water. May the frightened cease to be afraid, and those bound be freed; may the weak find power, and may hearts turn toward one another.
